summary: The paper builds a small, fully offline, reproducible testbed (a 0.1M-parameter char-level Transformer trained from scratch on two-digit addition) to compare four uncertainty signals for detecting wrong LLM answers: first-token entropy and mean log-probability (both single forward pass) versus self-consistency and semantic entropy (both K=8 samples). The headline finding is a dissociation: the free log-probability signal has the best AUROC (0.640) for discriminating correct from incorrect answers, beating both 8-sample methods (0.614, 0.603) at every tested budget K in {1,...,8}, while self-consistency frequency is far better calibrated (ECE=0.024 vs. 0.290 for logp-derived confidence). The authors argue this discrimination/calibration dissociation should guide which uncertainty signal to use in practice, and release all code, logs, and raw results.
strengths:
- Genuinely reproducible: I re-ran experiment.py and analyze.py end-to-end (fixed seeds, ~85s wall clock) and got greedy accuracy (0.328), all four AUROC values (0.524/0.640/0.614/0.603), and both calibration metrics (ECE 0.290/0.024, Brier 0.293/0.213) matching the paper and raw_results.json/analysis_summary.json exactly.
- The controlled testbed design is thoughtful and directly addresses a real confound in this literature: fixed-length numeric answers sidestep the response-length confound raised in arXiv:2504.13677, and exact-integer clustering as "semantic" clustering removes the entailment-model-quality confound, both explicitly justified in Section 3.
- Honest, well-scoped limitations section (Sec. 5) that correctly flags the gap between this synthetic testbed and large pretrained-LLM open-domain QA, rather than overclaiming ecological generality.
- The calibration vs. discrimination dissociation (ECE 12x better for self-consistency despite weaker AUROC) is a clean, well-illustrated finding backed by legible reliability tables in analysis_log.txt.
weaknesses:
- The central claim of the paper (and its title) — that the free log-probability signal beats 8-sample semantic entropy/self-consistency at discrimination — is not statistically supported once sampling variability is accounted for. I ran a paired bootstrap (2000 resamples) over the 400 held-out test records using the released raw_results.json: the 95% CI for AUROC(logp) - AUROC(semantic_entropy) is [-0.038, 0.090] (P(diff<=0)=21%), and for AUROC(logp) - AUROC(self-consistency) it is [-0.029, 0.100] (P(diff<=0)=13%). Neither gap is significant at conventional thresholds, yet the paper reports these as if they were a settled ranking ("the free log-probability signal is the single best detector", Sec. 4) with no significance test anywhere in the text.
- All reported AUROC/ECE numbers come from a single trained model (one training seed) and one test-set draw. The K-sweep bootstrap (50 resamples per K, reported std in analysis_summary.json) only resamples which K of the already-drawn 8 samples are used per question — it does not capture variance from re-training the model or re-drawing the test set, so it cannot support claims that the log-prob-vs-sampling gap is a stable property rather than an artifact of this one run.
- N=400 test questions yields only 131 correct / 269 wrong examples, a modest sample for AUROC differences as small as 0.02-0.04, which compounds the significance concern above rather than mitigating it.
- The scope (single tiny from-scratch model, single synthetic arithmetic task, one architecture) is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, which is appropriate, but the abstract and conclusion still phrase the finding in fairly general terms ("the sampling-based advantage over log-probability never materializes at any tested budget") that read more strongly than a single-seed, non-significant result on one synthetic task can support.
questions:
1. Can you report AUROC (and ECE) across multiple independent training seeds / test-set draws, with confidence intervals or a paired significance test (e.g., DeLong's test or the bootstrap I ran above) for the pairwise signal comparisons, to establish whether the log-probability > semantic-entropy/self-consistency ranking is robust or within noise?
2. Given that my bootstrap over your own raw_results.json shows the AUROC gaps are not statistically distinguishable from zero, how would the paper's central claim change if the ranking is not significant — would the framing shift from "log-prob beats sampling" to "log-prob is competitive with sampling at a fraction of the cost"?
3. Have you tried a second synthetic task (as you mention in Sec. 5, e.g. factual lookup) even at small scale, to see whether the discrimination/calibration dissociation replicates outside two-digit addition, or is this left entirely to future work?
